--- title: "Monte-Carlo Sampling Distributions of the Residual-Field Mean" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 --- ```{=html} ``` This report is **descriptive only**. It measures the sampling distribution of the residual-field domain mean under two designs — sampling that is uniform with respect to the analysis measure, and sampling by advected virtual floats — and displays those distributions. It constructs no test statistic and reports no $p$-value. Standard errors are given so the reader can judge what the Monte Carlo does and does not resolve. The hypothesis test of `theory.tex` is built on these ensembles in a companion report, [A Permutation Test for Preferential Sampling](permutation_test.html), which states the assumptions it needs, tests the ones that are testable, and finds two of the four rejected by the data. Everything is run over **two analysis regions**: Box B, in the North Atlantic Current, and Box A, in the subtropical gyre. They are set up identically and reported side by side throughout, in panel-tabsets on every figure and table, so the two can be compared under one construction. Because their fields differ $3.3\times$ in amplitude, the cross-box comparison is made on the standardized scale $B/\sigma_k$ and collected in a single section near the end. # Data and models **Field.** GLORYS12V1 reanalysis on its native $1/12^\circ$ grid. OHC is the $0$–$2000$ m depth integral of potential temperature against constant $c_p\rho$ (`code/ohc.py`), evaluated daily over 2010–2019. Cells enter the analysis only where $\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m *and* the integral is defined at every level, which is $92.4\%$ of Box B by area ($26{,}785$ cells) and $99.8\%$ of Box A ($34{,}863$ cells) — Box B loses its shelf edge, Box A is essentially all deep ocean. **Mean field.** Per-cell OLS of monthly OHC on $\{1,\,t,\,t^2,\,\sin 2\pi t,\,\cos 2\pi t,\, \sin 4\pi t,\,\cos 4\pi t\}$, fitted to the 1995–2019 monthly record with regressors averaged over each month to match what a monthly mean is. All cells share one design matrix, so the fit is a single pseudo-inverse. The residual field is $\tilde Z_k = \mathrm{OHC}_k - \hat m$, evaluated daily on the same mask. **Advection.** OceanParcels, park depth $1000$ m, driven by GLORYS daily $(u,v)$ over $15$–$50^\circ$ N, $70$–$30^\circ$ W. Floats advect continuously at park depth and record a position every $10$ days; there is no ascent, descent or surface drift, so a cycle is a position sample, not a simulated dive. Floats are deleted on leaving the velocity domain and retired at a lifespan drawn from the real Argo record for this region ($153$ deployments, median $1339$ d). **Estimation.** No model is fitted to the sampled values. $\hat Z$ is the unweighted mean of $\tilde Z_k$ at the profile positions, and $\bar Z_k$ is the exact $\mathbb{P}$-weighted domain mean of the same field; the comparison is arithmetic throughout. # The analysis domain Two analysis boxes sit inside the downloaded GLORYS region, both spanning $60^\circ$–$40^\circ$ W: **Box B** ($35$–$45^\circ$ N) straddles the North Atlantic Current and the Gulf Stream extension, and **Box A** ($22$–$34^\circ$ N) sits in the quiescent subtropical gyre. Temperature is downloaded over a common halo, from which the OHC truth and the fitted mean field are built; velocity is downloaded over a much larger region, because floats seeded near a box advect well outside it and return, and a float that leaves the velocity domain is lost from the experiment rather than merely lost from the box. ::: {#cell-fig-domain .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Analysis boxes inside the two downloaded GLORYS regions. Dashed: the velocity region driving advection, and the thetao region from which OHC truth and the mean field are built. Filled: the two analysis boxes.](mean_estimation_mc_files/figure-html/fig-domain-output-1.png){#fig-domain width=821 height=716} ::: ::: One pipeline is run over both boxes, with the same seeding law, margin, cycling cadence and replicate count; only the float number and spin-up length are tuned per box, and both are tuned to put the two arrays at matched density and matched equilibrium rather than to change what is measured. ::: {#cell-fig-bathy .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![GLORYS ocean depth over the advection domain. Left: deptho in km, capped at 6 km for display so the shelf break is resolved rather than compressed against the abyssal plain. Right: the ocean cells shallower than the 2000 m analysis cut, which are excluded from the OHC integral and from the measure P. Both analysis boxes are outlined. Land is grey in both panels.](mean_estimation_mc_files/figure-html/fig-bathy-output-1.png){#fig-bathy width=1402 height=605} ::: ::: @fig-bathy is why the analysis mask is not the whole box. OHC is integrated to $2000$ m, so a cell enters the estimand only where the water column reaches that depth; $88.7\%$ of the ocean cells in the advection domain do. The cut is not evenly distributed. **Box B loses $7.2\%$ of its area to it**, and that loss is concentrated in one corner: $99\%$ of its excluded cells lie north of $42^\circ$ N and $81\%$ west of $50^\circ$ W, on the Grand Banks and the Newfoundland shelf and rise. **Box A loses $0.08\%$** — $29$ cells, all isolated ridge and seamount tops in its eastern half. Median depth is $4.85$ km in Box B and $4.94$ km in Box A. Two consequences worth being explicit about. The depth cut is a *spatial* exclusion, so $\mathbb{P}$ and the estimand $\bar Z_k$ are defined on the retained region only, and a float profiling over the Grand Banks contributes nothing to $\hat Z$ even though it is inside the box's latitude–longitude bounds. And the exclusion is asymmetric between the boxes, so Box B's estimand is over a domain with a piece cut out of its northwest while Box A's is over essentially the full rectangle — which is one more respect in which the boxes are not identical, additional to the field and flow differences the comparison is about. The mask actually used is slightly stricter than the depth cut alone: it also requires the depth integral to be defined at every level, which drops a further $0.5\%$ of Box B and $0.15\%$ of Box A. Retained area is $92.35\%$ and $99.77\%$ against $92.83\%$ and $99.92\%$ from depth alone. ::: {#cell-fig-days .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Residual field Z on single unaveraged days, in GJ per m2. Days are selected independently for each component, so the panels here are not the same dates as the previous figure.](mean_estimation_mc_files/figure-html/fig-vel-v-output-1.png){#fig-vel-v width=1308 height=762} ::: ::: Three measurements from these two figures and the daily series behind them. **The flow is roughly twice as disperse in Box B, and that holds on every day, not just energetic ones.** Median daily $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}$ is $12.1$ cm/s eastward and $11.5$ northward in Box B against $5.5$ and $5.4$ in Box A, and the decade-wide range of that daily value is narrow in both — $9.7$–$14.8$ and $9.0$–$14.7$ in Box B, $4.5$–$7.0$ and $4.4$–$6.7$ in Box A. The 5th and 95th percentile columns are therefore much closer to each other than the two rows are, so the box, not the day, is what sets the scale. **Box B's structure is substantially standing, Box A's is substantially transient.** The $\mathbb{P}$-weighted spatial sd of the decade-mean velocity field is $4.11$ cm/s eastward and $2.37$ northward in Box B against $0.94$ and $0.61$ in Box A — a $4.4\times$ and $3.9\times$ gap, about twice the gap in the daily dispersion. As a fraction of each box's mean daily spatial sd, the persistent part is $0.34$ and $0.21$ in Box B against $0.17$ and $0.11$ in Box A. A standing pattern is what can bias an advected array the same way in every velocity year, which is what the column structure of the bias grids turns out to be. **Neither box has appreciable net transport.** The domain-mean velocity is within $\pm 1$ cm/s of zero on every one of the $3{,}650$ days in both components and both boxes (largest $0.996$ cm/s), so the contrast between the boxes is in spatial structure, not in bulk flow through the domain. Together with @fig-days this is the setup the two boxes were selected to contrast: they differ $3.3\times$ in field amplitude and $2.2\times$ in the daily spatial dispersion of the flow that samples it, with the standing component of that flow differing by about $4\times$. ::: {#cell-fig-meanfield .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Fitted mean field (quadratic trend plus annual and semiannual harmonics) at mid-month, 2015, in GJ per m2. The top two rows share one sequential scale so the residual's size relative to the OHC it came from is readable directly; the residual has its own diverging scale. The day shown is each box's median-spread day, as in the previous figure.](mean_estimation_mc_files/figure-html/fig-decomp3-output-1.png){#fig-decomp3 width=1024 height=1116} ::: ::: In @fig-decomp3 the identity $\mathrm{OHC} = \hat m + \tilde Z$ holds exactly on the analysis mask: the top row is reconstructed from the other two rather than re-integrated from temperature, and reproduces the GLORYS field bitwise. OHC runs $60$–$90$ GJ/m$^2$ and is almost entirely captured by the smooth mean field; $\tilde Z$ is a few GJ/m$^2$ of mesoscale structure. On the Box B day shown, domain-mean OHC is $67.9$ GJ/m$^2$ against a mean field of $66.5$ and a residual of $+1.45$. The mean field varies on two time scales, neither daily: the harmonics move the Box B domain mean by $3.80$ GJ/m$^2$ within a year ($1.50$ in Box A), the trend by $2.59$ across 2010–2019 ($0.96$), and consecutive days by $0.03$. Everything mesoscale and day-to-day is therefore left in $\tilde Z$. Three properties of $\tilde Z$ matter downstream. It is **strongly structured in space** at every quantile — even the 5th-percentile day carries a coherent front — which is what makes float position matter. That structure is **almost all of its variability**: Box B's median daily spatial spread is $6.63$ GJ/m$^2$ against a total $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z) = 6.81$ that also includes variation of the domain mean across days and years. And the two boxes differ several-fold in amplitude — daily spread spans $5.4$–$8.7$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B against $1.4$–$2.7$ in Box A — so bias and Monte Carlo error both scale with $\sigma_k$, and the boxes are comparable only on a standardized $B/\sigma_k$ scale. # Estimand, truth, and estimator Let $\mathbb{P}$ be the normalized area $\times$ time probability measure on the Box B analysis domain: the base measure is surface measure restricted to the wet native GLORYS cells ($\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m, intersected with the data support), $A_j = e1t_j\,e2t_j$, tensored with counting measure on the $365$ days of the year and normalized. The target is the residual field's domain mean, $$\bar Z_k \;=\; \int_{\mathcal{X}} \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P},$$ for each analysis year $k \in \{2010,\dots,2019\}$, where $\tilde Z_k$ is the year-$k$ OHC 0–2000 m field with the fitted mean field removed. A design is a finite point set $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \subset \mathcal{X}$; its estimator and bias are $$\hat Z^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde Z_k\!\left(x_i^{(l,d)}\right), \qquad B^{(l,d)}_k \;=\; \hat Z^{(l,d)}_k - \bar Z_k .$$ $\tilde Z_k$ is a simple function on the native $1/12^\circ \times$ daily grid, so evaluation at $x_i$ is the cell-day lookup of the cell *containing* $x_i$ — not an interpolation. No partition coarser than the data grid is introduced anywhere, so there is no quadrature remainder to carry. ::: {#tbl-truth .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

It is carried in @tbl-truth rather than assumed away. The dispersion columns are the $\sigma_k$ that any cross-box comparison of $B$ must be standardized by: $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k)$ runs $6.3$–$7.6$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B against $1.7$–$2.4$ in Box A, a factor of $3.3$. It also trends upward through the decade in Box B ($6.3$ in 2013 to $7.6$ in 2019) while Box A's is flat, so even within Box B the same raw bias means different things in different years. # The two ensembles Both use the same $7{,}500$ designs' worth of sample sizes, so they differ only in *where* the points sit. **Advective.** $307$ floats per replicate (Box A: $357$) seeded uniformly with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ — equal-area in latitude, uniform in longitude — over the analysis box widened by $8^\circ$ and clipped to the velocity domain, then advected through velocity year $l$. Only profiles falling inside the analysis box enter $\hat Z$. Ten velocity years $l \in \{2010,\dots,2019\}$, $750$ independent replicates each, each paired with all ten analysis years: $l = k$ is **aligned** (flow and field the same calendar year), all others **unaligned**. The Box A float count was chosen to match Box B's over-density relative to real Argo (@tbl-argo), so the two grids differ in flow and field, not in how heavily they are sampled. **Deployment runs from 540 days before the analysis year (Box A: 720), and the array is in equilibrium when the window opens.** A constant release rate cannot reach equilibrium here — the empirical lifespan median is $1339$ d in Box B and $1560$ d in Box A, so the stock is still climbing after $900$ d. The release density $f$ is instead solved as a smooth non-negative deconvolution against the measured in-box response $g(u) = \mathbb{P}(\text{in box at age } u)$, $$\min_{f \ge 0}\; \lVert f * g - 1 \rVert^2 \;+\; \lambda \lVert D^2 f \rVert^2 ,$$ which front-loads $80\%$ of releases into the spin-up so the in-box stock is flat across $[0,360)$ rather than ramping. The roughness penalty is load-bearing: the unpenalized solution is a sparse vertex of the feasible set, and releasing in bursts would rebuild the cohort structure in float age that this design exists to remove. Box A needs the longer spin because its floats leave the box far more slowly — $g(1080) = 0.14$ there, so the deconvolution has a longer memory to fill — and $720$ d is the longest spin the $2010$–$2019$ velocity archive supports for a $2010$ analysis year. @tbl-stock shows the schedule in action. **Uniform (U-full).** For each advective design, $n$ iid draws with cell $\propto A_j$ and $\mathrm{doy} \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{0,\dots,364\}$ — a genuine iid sample from $\mathbb{P}$, matched to that design's own $n$. "Contrast" is the aligned-minus-column mean in GJ/m$^2$, "contrast/se" divides the pooled value by the across-year standard error of the ten per-year contrasts. {#tbl-density} **The Box B effect survives; Box A still shows nothing.** Thinning removes $62\%$ of Box B's profiles and $58\%$ of Box A's, yet the pooled contrast retains $90\%$ of its magnitude in Box B ($-0.0529$ against $-0.0590$ GJ/m$^2$), stays negative in $10$ of $10$ analysis years, and remains $5.4$ across-year standard errors from zero. Box A moves from $+0.0030$ to $+0.0020$ GJ/m$^2$ and from four to five negative years, i.e. from indistinguishable-from-nothing to indistinguishable-from-nothing. Three quantities behave as they must, which is a check on the thinning as much as a result: - **Monte Carlo error grows as $n^{-1/2}$ and nothing else does.** The per-cell standard error rises $\times 1.63$ in Box B and $\times 1.55$ in Box A, against $\sqrt{307/118} = 1.61$ and $\sqrt{357/149} = 1.55$ predicted. - **The between-flow standard deviation does not move** — $0.0234 \to 0.0243$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B, $0.0063 \to 0.0057$ in Box A. It is a property of the flow field, not of how many floats sample it, so it should be invariant to thinning, and it is to within its own estimation noise. This is why the conclusion is robust: the report reads the diagonal against the between-flow scale, and that scale is unchanged. - **The design effect is unchanged** ($2.30 \to 2.20$ and $4.24 \to 4.15$), confirming it measures redundancy among a float's consecutive cycles rather than anything about array size. The uniform-reference check still passes at the thinned size in both boxes — $\mathbb{E}[B] = 0$ to within Monte Carlo error and widths matching $\sigma_k\sqrt{\overline{1/n}}$ — so the thinned ensembles are exercising the same verified pipeline. Two limitations. The thinned designs are **nested** inside the full ones, so the two ensembles are correlated; this is the right construction for asking "does the same experiment survive at lower density", but it is not an independent replicate, and a genuinely independent Argo-density ensemble would cost a fresh simulation. And Box B is density-matched **on the mean of per-year ratios** ($0.99$), not on the ratio of pooled means ($0.82$): real Box B stock triples across the decade ($8.1$ in 2011 to $31.0$ in 2017) while the simulated array is constant by construction, so the thinned array is over-dense before 2015 and under-dense after. Box A has no such trend and matches on both ($1.00$ and $0.98$). # Caveats - **Two boxes are not a design.** Box B and Box A differ in field structure, current speed, retention, latitude and coastline at once. The cross-box comparison of @tbl-contrast is a two-point contrast between two named regions, not a controlled manipulation of any one of those, and nothing here identifies which of them the diagonal displacement depends on. A gradient-varying sweep of boxes, or the same box under rescaled velocities, would be needed for that. - **One flow realization per year.** The $750$ replicates per cell are independent *deployments*; the velocity field is a single realization of that calendar year. Every standard error quoted is over deployment randomness only, which is exactly why the between-flow scale, not the Monte Carlo se, is the right yardstick for the diagonal. - **No inference is drawn.** The aligned-minus-column contrast is reported as a measurement. Turning Box B's ten negative signs into a $p$-value — or Box A's mixed signs into a statement of no effect — needs an exchangeability assumption over velocity years given the field, which this design cannot test; that is deferred. In particular, Box A's null result is an absence of a measured displacement at this resolution ($0.0015$–$0.0020\,\sigma_k$ per cell), not a demonstration that no displacement exists. - **The between-flow scale is estimated from nine numbers.** Each box's implied between-flow sd comes from the spread of nine unaligned cells net of their own Monte Carlo error, so it is itself noisy, and it degenerates when the two are comparable — as in Box A's 2018, where the netting leaves $0.0005$ GJ/m$^2$ and the resulting ratio is meaningless. - **$n$ is endogenous.** Retention inside the box is an outcome of the flow, so $\hat Z$ is a ratio estimator, the sample sizes differ systematically by velocity year (@fig-nsize), and the two ensembles are matched conditional on $n$. Design-weighted and profile-weighted averages of the temporal component differ because $n$ and day-of-year coverage are correlated; the design-weighted average is the one consistent with $\mathbb{E}[B]$ and is used throughout. This bites harder in Box A, where retention is stronger and the design effect correspondingly larger (@tbl-deff-a). - **The main arms are denser than real Argo, and constant where the real one grows.** The simulated standing stock is $2.6\times$ the real Box B stock on average and up to $5.2\times$ in the sparse early years, and it is held fixed at $41$–$44$ floats while the real stock swings by a factor of $3.8$ across the decade (@tbl-argo). This leaves $\mathbb{E}[B]$ alone — the bias of a sample mean under a given deployment law does not depend on how many floats realize it — but the per-design spreads shown outside @tbl-density are roughly $\sqrt{2.6}\approx 1.6$ times narrower than a real array in this box would produce, so read those widths as a lower bound on real sampling variability. @tbl-density resolves the substantive half of this by rerunning the estimator at real density; what it cannot fix is the *constancy*, since a design tracking the real deployment history would confound array growth with the flow-year contrast. Box A carries the same mismatch at $2.4\times$, which is close enough to Box B's $2.6\times$ that the two boxes' widths remain comparable to each other even though neither is comparable to a real array. - **Profiling is synchronized across floats.** Trajectory output is written on a fixed cadence from the run start, so all virtual floats profile on the same $36$ days of the year rather than each cycling from its own deployment date, as real Argo floats do (@tbl-stock). The realized day-of-year marginal is therefore supported on $36$ atoms rather than spread over the year, which is part of why the temporal component varies so little across designs. It does not bias $\hat Z$ on its own — the epochs are near-uniformly spaced — but it understates the temporal diversity a real array would have, and any statement here about day-of-year coverage should be read with that in mind. - **The spin-up ages the array.** Holding the standing stock flat requires releasing $\sim\!80\%$ of floats before the analysis year, which leaves the in-box age distribution older than a constant-rate array would give. The alternative — accepting the ramp — puts a far larger artefact into the day-of-year marginal, so this is the lesser distortion, but it is a distortion. - **$\tilde Z$ inherits the mean-field fit.** The seasonal residual driving the temporal term is itself what the trend-plus-harmonics basis failed to absorb; a different mean-field specification would move it. @tbl-truth reports the fit's leftover offset per year, which is largest in 2010–2014.
